data.title: MDA SPACE COMPLETES ACQUISITION OF BLUE CANYON TECHNOLOGIES
data.description:
MDA SPACE COMPLETES ACQUISITION OF BLUE CANYON TECHNOLOGIES

MDA SPACE COMPLETES ACQUISITION OF BLUE CANYON TECHNOLOGIES

PR Newswire

TORONTO, Nov. 27, 2026

TORONTO, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MDA Space Ltd. (TSX: MDA) (NYSE: MDA) (the "Company"), a trusted mission partner to the rapidly expanding global defence and space industry, today announced that it has completed its previously announced acquisition of Blue Canyon Technologies (BCT) LLC, a U.S.-based spacecraft and satellite component manufacturer and mission services provider, formerly part of RTX.

BCT brings 400 highly skilled employees in the Denver, Colorado space and aerospace hub, and more than 95 spacecraft launched and 4,300 products on orbit. Its addition to MDA Space provides the company with a strategic business and manufacturing footprint to capitalize on growing demand in the U.S. government market for defence space missions. With the close of the acquisition, BCT will be rebranded as MDA Space and operate as MDA Space USA. 

"I want to welcome the Blue Canyon Technologies team to MDA Space. The addition of BCT to MDA Space adds a strong and established business and team with domestic manufacturing capability that is ideally positioned to accelerate our growth strategy in the expanding U.S. defence market," said Mike Greenley, CEO of MDA Space. "Securing these strategic benefits on an accretive basis with a profitable and cash-generating business makes this an ideal fit for MDA Space global expansion and continued shareholder value creation." 

ABOUT MDA SPACE
Building the space between proven and possible, MDA Space (TSX:MDA) (NYSE:MDA) is a trusted mission partner to the global defence and space industry. A robotics, satellite systems and geointelligence pioneer with a 55-year+ story of world firsts and more than 450 missions, MDA Space is a global leader in communications satellites, Earth and space observation, and space exploration and infrastructure. The global MDA Space team of more than 4,000 space experts has the knowledge and know-how to turn an audacious customer vision into an achievable mission — bringing to bear a one-of-a-kind mix of experience, engineering excellence and wide-eyed wonder that's been in our DNA since day one. For those who dream big and push boundaries on the ground and in the stars to change the world for the better, we'll take you there. For more information, visit mda.space.

Nvidia's stock soared this week, but was still down nearly 28% for November and 21% for 2026

The return of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang as the company's CEO on Nov. 23 helped drive the entire U.S. stock market higher this week.

The broad U.S. stock indexes were all green early on Friday, as investors were closer to capping off a week of remarkable gains, sparked by Jensen Huang's return as CEO. Still, the gains only partially offset the previous week's declines.

data.title: My husband secretly sends his ex-wife $1,500 a month after she lost her job. We have $2.4 million saved. Has he lied by omission?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'He explained that he wasn't trying to hide the payment, but his former wife lost her job in a medical billing company'

"We have roughly $2.4 million shared for retirement and we are in good shape, but I don't see how this justifies that secret $1,500-a-month payment." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I have read some of your articles about financial infidelity and I have a doozy for you. I was going through my husband's belongings, looking for his life insurance policy, and I found a standing order to his ex-wife for $1,500 a month. This has been going on since 2023, which I now calculate comes to $18,000 a year he has paid his ex-wife.

This has been going on all the while we have been planning for retirement. I'm 61 and he is 64 and we have three children and four grandchildren. Two of our children are my stepchildren. We have roughly $2.4 million shared for retirement and we are in good shape, but I don't see how this justifies that secret $1,500-a-month payment.

I asked my husband about it, not in a confrontational way, but in a sort of surprised and disappointed way. He explained that he wasn't trying to hide the payment, but his former wife lost her job in a medical billing company, and she rents a one-bedroom apartment. This covers the rent, basically. He also pointed out that they were married for 20 years.

He also explained that his ex-wife was a homemaker while he worked seven days a week, and that they barely had a moment to spare in the first few years of their marriage. He feels like he owes her. He said he will stop the payments once her finances have stabilized. He feels responsible for the mother of his children. They are in their 30s, and could also help their mother out.

My husband also argued that $1,500 accounts for less than 1% of our savings. True, but that would also add up to $90,000 over five years, and so far he has given her $54,000. I feel like three years is an adequate amount of time for her to get on her feet again. I asked him to consider how he would feel if I had privately given $1,500 a month to an ex-boyfriend.

He said he's trying to be a good person to everybody. Maybe I am jealous, but has he lied to me by omission?

A Surprised Wife

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: 'I like the idea of a big return': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?

Her contribution to their marriage should have been taken care of during their divorce. It's not a lifetime debt that must be repaid at the expense of your relationship.

Dear Wife,

As always, the cover-up is worse than the crime or, in this case, the supposed charity. So, yes, he was lying by omission. But it was an honorable lie.

Spending $1,500 a month on an ex-wife should require discussion. You don't mention whether you have separate/marital funds, or whether you have a joint account for household expenses, and - who knows - you may have understood had he sought out your counsel/input. But it's the secrecy that bites, and the discovery naturally damages your trust.

Over five years, you point out that his ex-wife would receive $90,000. That is equivalent to 3.75% of your total retirement savings. To put that in context, you would probably pay a financial adviser 1% of your portfolio to manage it. And, yes, you could do a lot with that money, including pay for school fees and vacations.

Being a good husband and a good citizen sometimes requires having difficult conversations, like telling friends, an ex-wife, or even family members "no" if they ask for money, whether for a gift or a loan. In this case, it's hard to see that monthly stipend as a loan that will be returned at some point, especially if there's no written agreement about a payment plan.

You could do a lot with that money, including pay for school fees and vacations.

The fact that he's giving such a large sum of money to his ex-wife of 20 years absolutely makes this worse, not better. Supporting an ex-wife without telling your current partner is being a bad husband and a bad ex-husband. After all, the whole point of divorce is to sever emotional, financial and legal ties. That's why divorce is painful, expensive and traumatic.

The intention is an understandable one. Your husband, you say, pointed out that he maintained his career while his wife was a homemaker. Research by sociologist Thomas Leopold has found "large and persistent gender differences" in divorce where women experience "disproportionate losses in household income," which increases their risk of poverty.

Leopold concluded that men's long-term disproportionate strain of divorce is transient, whereas the impact on women's economic future is chronic." He made that conclusion despite his findings that both men and women experience similar outcomes of subjective economic well-being over the medium term as related to emotional, mental health and physical health.

Don't miss: 'I don't feel sorry for myself': I'm 64 and will be renting for the rest of my life - but here's why I'm still hopeful

Financial infidelity

I have no doubt that his ex-wife sacrificed a lot during their marriage, including aspects of her career. Stay-at-home parents do a lot of work that is not always recognized by society as having economic value. But her contribution to their marriage should have been taken care of during their divorce. It's not a lifetime debt that must be repaid at the expense of your relationship.

He's also missing a broader point. This is not a conversation or a personal conflict about being a good husband versus friend. It is about navigating the world as a team, as a couple, and as a married couple who are in their 60s and planning on retiring. It's difficult to do that if one party is unilaterally making financial decisions behind the other person's back.

The $1,500-a-month payment does two things: First, it acts as an incentive for his ex-wife not to find work anytime soon; second, it creates an emotional relationship, as well as a financial one (that emotional relationship is heightened by the secrecy). Whether your husband wants to acknowledge it or not, this is a classic case of financial infidelity.

The gift to his ex-wife creates an emotional relationship, as well as a financial one.

It's not so unusual, but that doesn't make it any better. Roughly 45% of people admit to financial infidelity, according to a poll released last year by Bankrate, the personal-finance site. The most common form relates to secret spending, followed by secret debt, secret credit cards, and secret bank accounts. The key word is "secret."

Three years is not the kind of "temporary" that rings true. Twenty years is a long time to spend with a partner, married or not, but I'm curious to know whether his ex-wife has found another job or intends to find alternative work. This is an opportunity to talk about (a) whether the money will be repaid, (b) when the payments will stop (they can't go on forever) and (c) what happens next.

By feeling jealousy, you are buying into his financial infidelity as an acceptable act, rather than focusing on his secrecy. Why does your husband have this disease to please? Why does he have to be all things to all people? Why can't he say no? Why does he still have an obligation to his ex-wife and mother of his children, even if they were together for 20 years?

You can't plan a future with someone who doesn't put all their cards on the table. Well, you can. But it makes the planning all the more difficult.

Related: My sister moved in with our mother, 78, and says she deserves the $925,000 family home. Is she right?

data.title: My friends play 'credit-card roulette' to see who pays for dinner - but one 'winner' still Venmoed me afterward. Should I say something?
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

'I was stunned! I've lost my fair share, and won my fair share, and truly believe it all evens out over time.'

"I went to sleep thinking it was another monthly dinner where I dodged a bullet."

Dear Dollar Signs,

I'm a 31-year-old male living in the NYC Metro area. My friends and I often go to dinner or a happy hour after a workday, and as you might guess, a five-person dinner and drinks in Manhattan routinely goes for $300 to $400.

My friends like to gamble, and we often play "credit-card roulette," aka a game where the waiter randomly selects one of our cards, and the "winner" has to pay the entire dinner bill.

I've lost my fair share, and won my fair share, and truly believe it all evens out over time. After a recent dinner, a friend who doesn't normally join us "won" credit-card roulette. He paid, and I went to sleep thinking it was another monthly dinner where I dodged a bullet.

The next morning, he sends me a Venmo charge for my share of the dinner. Considering I don't flinch whenever I have to pay a giant dinner bill, I was stunned! We explained the rules beforehand, but it appears as though he thought the "punishment" was to pay, and then chase down the Venmos later.

Do I say something to him, or do I just pay for my share?

Stunned

Dear Stunned,

Your comfort with picking up the tab on such a hefty bill seems to hinge on the longevity of your relationship with these people. I tend to agree with you about winning some and losing some: When you've been friends with someone for years, I do believe that it all evens out.

However, your friend is not part of this longstanding "credit-card roulette" routine. Perhaps this was a simple misunderstanding, as you said, where he simply thought that whoever gets picked is only paying upfront, maybe to score points if they have a rewards card, with the intent to track down payments later.

He might also just feel a bit weird paying into a system from which he is not benefiting, financially or socially. If I was invited to dinner with a group of people for the first time, and then saddled with a $400 bill, I might feel a type of way, too.

You ask if you should say something, or pay him. I say both. Shell out the $80 or so that he requested, and then, if you plan on inviting him back to one of these dinners, tactfully tell him that he misunderstood the game, and explain that if he plays, then he is potentially on the hook for the entire check. And have the conversation in person, says Emily Post Institute etiquette expert Lizzie Post.

"A text leaves too much to the imagination to the person on the other end," she says. Context is often lost when you're not speaking in person. "It's like dropping a bomb into their world. Even if you think it's going to be funny, there is not enough of your own context ... to make it land in a joking way."

How to confront your friend

I understand your hesitation. Splitting tabs often causes friction in friend groups: 33% of Gen Z consumers say settling shared bills creates stress or anxiety, according to recent data from Zelle. And 25% say repayment issues have caused damage to long-term relationships.

This also comes as dining out keeps getting more expensive. 32% of diners say menu prices are too expensive for the quality, according to the 2025 U.S. dining-out report from market-research firm YouGov. And 37% of surveyed diners said they were going out to eat less often than they did the year before, with most citing higher prices as their main reason for staying in.

If you don't plan to invite him to dinner again, then just pay your share and move on. But, if you'd like him to be part of the group, a short conversation is worth having.

Despite me postulating that your friend was uncomfortable with paying the whole bill, I wouldn't go into the conversation assuming that. It might be a good idea to take the blame on yourself, and say that you're not sure you explained the rules quite clearly.

Keep the tone light, Post says, like this is a silly misunderstanding, not a social faux pas. Money is touchy. You don't want him to feel like you're saying he is cheap or obtuse.

"Call up and say, 'Hey I saw your Venmo. Typically, the person who gets picked just foots the whole bill, which can be a lot - but it's also awesome when it's not you,'" she says.

As the saying goes, "Honesty without tact is cruelty." So, be kind and empathic to the fact that, yes, it does suck when your card gets chosen. But, it's very fun when it doesn't.

Be prepared for the conversation to perhaps reveal things about your friend that you didn't know or assume, says Anna Goldfarb, the author of "Modern Friendship: How to Nurture Our Most Valued Connections."

Your friend might not be able to afford a $400 bill (I know there were times in my life when that would have bankrupted me). Or, maybe this type of "gambling" just isn't fun for him.

"The person who sent the Venmo requests after the meal probably values fairness highly, which is why they charged everyone for their share," Goldfarb says. "The recipient of the Venmo request probably values respecting the rules of the game more."

If they react stunned or put off by you clarifying the rules, I would probably find a different way to socialize with him.

What about the waiter?

Out of curiosity, I spoke with some service-industry workers to see how they felt about groups playing "credit-card roulette" when it's time to settle up. If it was something restaurant staff hated, then my advice would have been to stop the practice altogether.

But after chatting with various servers working at restaurants in Times Square, a place with a notoriously diverse demographic of customers, I found that they actually don't mind.

"It's fun. I love it. It makes me more engaged with the table. It's a playful thing," Kevin Reyes, a server at Tsuru Ton Tan, told me.

"I don't care. I think it's a bit of fun. I've never had any awkwardness with it," Lucy Craven, a server at Langan's said.

And I guess that is the whole point: "Credit-card roulette" is supposed to be fun. Happy hour and dinner with your friends is supposed to be fun. If this is not your friend's idea of a good time, then you can still invite them to hang out - but perhaps when the stakes are not quite so high.

Write to Dollar Signs at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

data.title: Nvidia's stock has tumbled 28% over one chaotic month. The next big test lies in the week ahead
data.description:
An earlier version incorrectly stated when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will speak to Congress. By Bill Peters

Jensen Huang faces tough questions from Congress this week. Good luck pinning him down, one analyst says.

This handout photo posted on Nvidia's official X account on Nov. 23 shows reinstated CEO Jensen Huang reacting to an ovation from employees upon his return to the company headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif.

After a month unlike any other for Nvidia, the chip maker at the heart of the artificial-intelligence boom and the stock market faces even more drama in the week ahead.

Newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang will face harsh questioning from U.S. lawmakers from both parties next week in Washington, D.C. During that stretch, Nvidia (NVDA) will also hold a large developer conference in the same city, which could shed light on new products.

In both events, Nvidia will try to repair its image and articulate its path forward, after Huang resigned earlier this month following reports that he had extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a spy for China.

Nvidia's stock has dropped 28% in November as of Thursday morning, putting it on track for its worst monthly performance since it lost 32% in April 2022. That decline comes even after an 17% rally so far this week.

Huang's ouster, which lasted a little more than a week, initially lopped more than $1 trillion from Nvidia's market value. And it deepened concerns over national security, the lengths taken and possible exceptions made to restore Huang to his old job on Monday, and an economy and stock market seemingly dependent on one executive.

Huang is set to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews with three House committees on Tuesday. He will also appear before the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs on Thursday.

During those hearings, analysts say, lawmakers are almost certain to ask about Nvidia's relationship with China and the U.S. government, and what sensitive information Huang may have handed over to China, which looks for a leg up in the global AI race. There will also likely be questions about what Nvidia knew, if anything, about China's alleged access to its high-end chips - via smuggling, routing them through other nations or remote access - and the money behind it.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Jay Goldberg, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners who covers semiconductors, said that Huang appeared to have support among Nvidia's employees and shareholders. Attitudes in Congress - from Democrats worried about President Donald Trump and aggressive AI development to Republicans worried about economic threats from China - were more frigid.

"[T]he one thing that Democrats and Republicans can agree on is that the greatest entrepreneur of all time is somehow a target," he said. "Not to excuse what he's done, but everything's upside-down right now."

That target may have gotten bigger, after Bloomberg reported Friday that some of Nvidia's newer chips have turned up at a data center in China that's tied to someone Huang had an affair with.

Still, Huang, if nothing else, knows how to work a room, Goldberg said.

"Having had the pleasure of trying to pin Jensen down on a live-mic Q&A session at an investor event in the past: Good luck to them," he said of lawmakers' efforts to press Huang for specifics. "He is incredibly charismatic and knows how to handle a microphone."

John Blank, chief equity strategist at Zacks Investment Research, also said Huang was the most personable of the tech titans. But he said Huang understood the gravity of the situation.

"To some degree, he is somewhat humbled from the last two weeks, and I expect him to take it seriously and be pretty straightforward here," Blank said. "I would be surprised if he was flip and super arrogant at this point in time."

Huang's return to the top post - with President Donald Trump's help - launched Nvidia's stock to its biggest one-day percentage gain in 23 years. But shares fell on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Blank said some investors may be short-covering during next week's hearings, as they recalibrate their bets based on any news. But he and other analysts said Nvidia's stock is unlikely to be affected by the hearing, at least in the short term.

"This is the opening salvo of at least a year of stuff, and the market's pricing in plenty of surprises for all of this," Blank said.

Huang and Nvidia still face investigations from Nvidia's board, Congress and regulators. Trump has said the U.S. government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk" to national security. But more scrutiny could come when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Senate's current minority leader, has said Democrats would investigate "any wrongdoing" by Nvidia or the Trump administration, and look into discussions between the U.S. and China about Huang, and Trump's Nvidia stockholdings. The White House has said Trump's investment portfolio is managed independently, and that neither Trump nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input" on the portfolio, according to multiple reports.

Schumer also called for stronger export controls. Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas has also criticized Nvidia's decision to bring Huang back to the company.

Other issues still hang over Nvidia's stock, such as the costs and financing of the AI buildout and Nvidia's role as a financier to other parts of the AI industry. Huang's remarks could affect the broader semiconductor industry if he reveals more details about the flow of chips into China, Blank said.

The hearings are likely to overshadow Nvidia's GTC conference, which runs from Monday through Thursday. Prior to this month's blowup at the company, Huang was set to deliver the keynote on Tuesday - the same day he appears before the House committees.

According to CNBC, Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, was scheduled to speak in place of Huang. Were Huang to make an appearance, analysts said, it could give him a chance to rally the company. But there were also risks.

"It would be lost in the noise and the public spectacle of his return, so I don't know if it would be all that productive for him to be at GTC from a technical standpoint," said Cody Acree, an analyst at StoneX.

Acree said he would be watching for updates on the rollout of Nvidia's Rubin Ultra chips, seen as a key component of powering agentic AI. Otherwise, it would be an event for networking and discussions about things like copper connectivity.

"Up until very recently, semiconductors were so boring," Goldberg said. "There have been very few instances in which my CEOs ended up in front of Congress. So, brave new world."

-Bill Peters

data.title: Artificial intelligence usage is exploding, yet spending is stalling. Why a foundational rule of economics is breaking.
data.description:
By Jules Rimmer

The so-called 'Jevons Paradox' is breaking down in the second half of 2026

The deceleration in spending growth on AI tokens is a major cause for concern among the frontier model developers

So-called Jevons Paradox - the 19th century theory which when applied to artificial intelligence holds that as token prices fall, usage increases enough to increase overall spend - is in danger of being broken.

So far in 2026, for instance, the volume of tokens used - each unit of compute - has risen 44 times - but the total spend is only up 7.6 times, according to OpenRouter, an aggregator of AI platforms.

In the third quarter that elasticity fell from 5.5 to 1.6, and fourth quarter-to-date that figure has dropped again to 1.2.

In a blog post OpenRouter says demand for the compute capacity is strong but buyers are able to deploy the resources more efficiently, without increasing their budget.

There is a precedent for this. In December 2024 and November 2025 there were dips but both of these were followed by recoveries once new model launches were rolled out.

Cheaper inference, by which it costs less money and requires less power to run a trained artificial intelligence model, does still generate huge usage, but it isn't proving that spending boost as enterprises become more conscious of their total AI spend.

Some of this uncertainty has been reflected in the perfomance of frontier model lab Anthropic (ANT). After listing at $83 last week the shares rallied as high as $115 but fell below the issue price this week. In early trading on Friday, the stock rose nearly 6%, topping $87.

OpenAI is not yet publicly traded, but minority investor SoftBank (JP:9984) has dropped 32% this year. On the crypto platform Hyperliquid, a token for OpenAI has gone from indicating a market cap of $1.7 trillion to now indicating a valuation of $1.2 trillion.

-Jules Rimmer

data.title: “An attack on public health care & the nurses who deliver it” OCHU-CUPE blasts Ford government for voting against safe nurse staffing legislation
data.description:
“An attack on public health care & the nurses who deliver it” OCHU-CUPE blasts Ford government for voting against safe nurse staffing legislation

Ontario PC MPPs voted against the NDP legislation for nurse-to-patient ratios in hospitals on Thursday

The largest hospital union in the province is slamming the Ontario Progressive Conservatives for “attacking public health care and the nurses who deliver it” after government MPPs voted down legislation that would have guaranteed safe nurse staffing in hospitals.

On Thursday, the Ontario PCs voted against Bill 19, the Patient-to-Nurse Ratios for Hospitals Act, introduced by NDP MPP France Gélinas. The bill would have set staffing standards for various hospital units, based on models already in place in British Columbia, Nova Scotia and California and being implemented in Manitoba.

“The government is gaslighting the nurses who work in our public hospitals. Three in four nurses say they fear their patients could be harmed because of understaffing, and the government’s answer is to refuse even to allow the bill to go to a committee of the legislature to be studied. This issue will only build as patients and their families and nurses demand safe staffing, knowing that safer care models exist in other provinces,’ ” said Michael Hurley, president of CUPE’s Ontario Council of Hospital Unions (OCHU-CUPE), which represents about 50,000 health care workers, including 16,000 nurses.

“Staffing hospitals with the bare minimum number of nurses per unit has been responsible for unnecessary deaths, a higher rate of readmission and a slower recovery rate for patients. For the government to double down on deliberate understaffing is completely unacceptable,” he said.

Earlier this week, OCHU-CUPE released an academic study and a new poll of nurses exposing the hospital staffing crisis. The findings are alarming: only nine per cent of nurses say their units are always fully staffed, and 78 per cent fearing their patients are at risk.

“Our government had an opportunity to prioritize patient safety, support nurses and strengthen health care for our communities. Nurses cannot continue working in survival mode and be expected to provide the quality of care our patients deserve,” said Angela Hodgson, a registered practical nurse and chair of OCHU-CUPE’s RPN committee.

The evidence is clear on the issue, says the union, highlighting research showing that nurse-to-patient ratios lower death rates, improve job satisfaction among nurses and save health care costs.

data.title: Help Heal Veterans’ The Healing Journey™ Wins Silver and Bronze at the 2026 Anthem Awards
data.description:
Help Heal Veterans’ The Healing Journey™ Wins Silver and Bronze at the 2026 Anthem Awards

National recognition celebrates the power of creativity and shines a light on the invisible wounds of war and veterans’ journeys toward healing

Help Heal Veterans (Heal Vets), the nation’s leader in providing therapeutic craft kits to veterans and active-duty service members, has earned two prestigious honors at the 6th Annual Anthem Awards. The organization’s immersive art installation, The Healing Journey™, received a Silver Anthem Award for Community Space and a Bronze Anthem Award for Mental & Behavioral Health, both in the Health category.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261127358911/en/

The Healing Journey by Artist Allison McClain

The recognitions place The Healing Journey among this year’s distinguished social impact initiatives, selected from more than 2,500 entries from 43 countries.

Created by artist Allison McClain, The Healing Journey is a visual storytelling experience that brings to life the emotional and psychological challenges veterans may face during and after military service. The installation illustrates a service member’s journey of service, struggle, and healing, highlighting the vital role creative expression can play in emotional recovery.

The Healing Journey is currently on display at Help Heal Veterans’ headquarters in Winchester, California, and its newly opened Creative Engagement Center at Liberty Station in San Diego. Heal Vets will also showcase The Healing Journey at Creative Engagement Centers across the country, including locations in San Antonio and Temple, Texas, and Chicago, Illinois, bringing its powerful message of healing through creativity to more veterans and communities nationwide.

“These awards recognize the experiences of the men and women who have served our country, including the struggles that are not always visible,” said Capt. Joe McClain, USN (Ret.), CEO of Help Heal Veterans. “For more than 55 years, we’ve seen how working with your hands and engaging in creative activities can provide comfort, purpose, and a sense of accomplishment. Our hope is that The Healing Journey inspires greater understanding of the challenges veterans face and the many ways we can support them on their path toward healing.”

The Anthem Awards recognize individuals, organizations, and initiatives making a meaningful impact on communities around the world. Presented by the Webby Awards, the competition honors purpose-driven work across a range of social impact categories.

“The work of social impact doesn’t pause when conditions get harder, and this year’s Anthem Winners proved it,” said Anthem Awards General Manager, Patricia McLoughlin. “Facing new challenges, they kept building, kept organizing, and kept delivering for the people and causes they serve. They set a new standard for good, one defined as much by persistence as by results.”

data.title: BAE Systems Secures $6 Billion in Combat-Vehicle Contracts For Several European Nations
data.description:
By Mauro Orru

BAE Systems said it had secured $6 billion in contracts to supply hundreds of combat vehicles to several European nations as they seek to buttress their armed forces amid high geopolitical tensions.

The U.K. arms maker said it would provide more than 400 CV90 combat vehicles to the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Lithuania under contracts awarded through separate purchase-order agreements.

The group said support systems, training, spare parts, special tools and test equipment were part of the deal and that the vehicles and components would be produced through a distributed supplier network across those nations.
